replying_to: Replying to Adversarial Attack across Datasets
display_title: Official Review of Paper2341 by Reviewer 65Ly

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work points out one of the limitations of transfer-based attacks. Namely, the assumption therein is usually unrealistic as the attacker may not know the dataset used by the victim model. To overcome the limitation, this work proposes to build a virtual surrogate model with multiple datasets and models. The process to build the surrogate model is formulated as meta-learning process.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
The authors work on an interesting question, which is of importance to the community.
The meta-learning based formulation as a solution is novel to me.

Weaknesses:
1. The biggest concern for me is the efficiency of the proposed approach. To build such a ‘virtual’ surrogate model, the authors have to train K models on N datasets respectively. The building process can be expensive. I guess that that is why there don’t test and report the results on ImageNet-1K dataset. However, almost all other approaches listed in this paper work pretty well on ImageNet-1K dataset.

2. The effectiveness of the proposed ICE can be affected by the following factors: model architecture difference, datasets, label sets, and input sizes. The impact of all these factors should be studied. ICE could be very sensitive to some of them. Especially, the authors report the results on CIFAR10 dataset where the datasets used to build surrogate models is overlapped with the target one. To what extent the overlap will affect the final transferability?

3. The authors have a good summary of different attack approaches in Tab. 1. Regarding this table, I have a question about the input resolution. The author states that other attack approaches require information about the input resolution while the proposed one does not. Why it is so? For other approaches, they can create transferable adversarial examples at a different scale. I assume it is the responsibility of the target model to resize the adversarial examples to a specific size (which is true in real-world applications). If it is not the case, what size of adversarial example the proposed ICE should create to attack the target model?

4. In the experimental section 4.5.4, the study shows that the performances of ICE will be damaged by the increase of the number of gradient ascent steps. What about if we use more attack iterations? Is the transferability of the adversarial examples decreased further?

5. In some cases, the authors also report the results on epsilon= 8/255 (a popular setting). Most experiments are conducted on the setting where the perturbation range is epsilon= 15/255. Is there a particular reason for this choice?

6. In Figure 5 in the appendix, the authors visualize the created noise created by ICE. They are visually different from the ones created by others. Does the difference tell us anything about the effectiveness of the proposed method? Can the author comment on why it is different?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper works on an interesting problem, which is also relevant to ICLR community. The proposed solution is also novel to some degree. However, the limitation of the proposed approach is not addressed. The ablation study on the proposed method is not comprehensive enough. Hence, I rate this paper blew the acceptance threshold.

display_title: Response to question: In Figure 5 in the appendix, the authors visualize the created noise created by ICE. They are visually different from the ones created by others. Can the author comment on why it is different?

content.title: Response to question: In Figure 5 in the appendix, the authors visualize the created noise created by ICE. They are visually different from the ones created by others. Can the author comment on why it is different?
content.comment:
It is very interesting to see that the perturbation noise generated by ICE differs greatly from those generated by the other methods.
The possible reason for this phenomenon is that ICE is trained to maximize the prediction entropy without using labels.
In other words, **ICE needs to disturb the input image without knowing the groundtruth classification information, which forces ICE to learn perturbation pattern that correlates little with groundtruth information.**

In Figure 5, we can see that **ICE generates similar perturbation noises for different input images, which means ICE may learn a perturbation pattern that is generalizable across different image categories.**
In our opinion, learning a generalizable perturbation pattern may be a straightforward way for ICE to solve generalized transfer attack.
The visualization may remind us that it is possible to find a universal perturbation pattern that can solve generalized transfer attack, which can be regarded as another contribution of ICE.
The visualization may also inspire us to better understand and improve the robustness issue of DNNs.

content.title: Response to question: The authors also report the results on epsilon= 8/255 (a popular setting). Most experiments are conducted on the setting where the perturbation range is epsilon= 15/255. Is there a particular reason for this choice?
content.comment:
In existing transfer attack methods, $\epsilon$=15/255 or 16/255 is a more popular setting than 8/255.
For example, the official papers of baselines (MI, DI, TI, IR, AEG) commonly set $\epsilon$=15/255 or 16/255 by default.
This is because transfer attack is more difficult than white-box and query-based black-box attack.
Smaller $\epsilon$ will produce a much lower attack success rate.
**We therefore follow the most popular setting of $\epsilon$=15/255 or 16/255 to evaluate our method.**

display_title: Response to question: To build such a ‘virtual’ surrogate model, the authors have to train K models on N datasets respectively. The building process can be expensive.

content.title: Response to question: To build such a ‘virtual’ surrogate model, the authors have to train K models on N datasets respectively. The building process can be expensive.
content.comment:
Thanks for your question.
**Training K models on N datasets is an indispensable step for all methods but not only for the proposed ICE.**
Given the trained K source models and N source datasets, the proposed ICE
needs to further prepare another model (universal surrogate model) for generalized transfer attack.

But in inference, ICE costs fewer computation resources than baselines to disturb input images, which is another advantage of ICE over baselines.
This is because the proposed ICE needs to confuse only the universal surrogate model in inference, while the baselines need to simultaneously confuse all the K source models.
Confusing K source models needs to calculate the gradient in all the K source models while confusing a single universal surrogate model needs to calculate the gradient only in one model.
**As Section A.6 introduces, ICE greatly saves the inference cost compared with baselines.**

display_title: Response to Reviewer 65Ly

content.title: Response to Reviewer 65Ly
content.comment:
## Question:
The effectiveness of the proposed ICE can be affected by the following factors: model architecture difference, datasets, label sets, and input sizes. The impact of all these factors should be studied. 
### Response:
The experiments in Table 2 have studied the factors of the number of source models, the number of source datasets, the input size.
For example, Table 2 demonstrates that given either more source models or more source datasets, the performance of the proposed ICE can be improved clearly.
Furthermore, Table 2 also shows that the input size of the source dataset influences the performances of not only ICE but also baselines.
For instance, the comparison between the Cifar-10+Tiered$\_{V56}+$(ResNet-18) row and the Cifar-10+Tiered$\_{T84}+$(ResNet-18) row indicates that the more similarities between the source dataset resolution and the target dataset resolution, the higher the performances of the proposed ICE and the baselines.

## Question:
The authors have a good summary of different attack approaches in Tab.1. Regarding this table, I have a question about the input resolution. The author states that other attack approaches require information about the input resolution while the proposed one does not. Why it is so? 
### Response: 
Thanks for your question.
1. Because of the commonly used fully-connect or pooling layers, source models in transfer attack usually can only handle input resolutions with little variety. For example, ImageNet models commonly are difficult to directly predict small (32x32) resolution images. Therefore, the other attack approaches need to know the input resolution of the target model and then prepare proper source models to disturb the images that will be fed into the target model. In our work, the proposed ICE can handle input resolutions with a large variety.
2. Image resizing is happened before feeding the images into target models. Generalized transfer attack requires the attacker to directly disturb any intercepted images that have been resized for different target models. Then the disturbed images will fool the target models.

## Question:
In the experimental section 4.5.4, the study shows that the performances of ICE will be damaged by the increase of the number of gradient ascent steps. What about if we use more attack iterations? Is the transferability of the adversarial examples decreased further?
### Response:
Yes, ICE will perform worse when increasing the number of gradient ascent steps in the inner-loop when training the universal surrogate model. For example, when there are 6 gradient ascent steps in the inner-loop, the performance of ICE will be 43.8%, 56.6%, 49.2%, 46.7%, 44.8%, 48.8%, and 60.9% on MobileNet-V3, VGG-16, ResNet-18, ResNet-34, SeResNet-26, and DenseNet-26, respectively.
When there are 7 gradient ascent steps in the inner-loop,  ICE will not converge. 

The main reason is that the bi-level optimization needs to unroll the inner steps, so increasing inner steps (attack steps) will make it harder to train.

replying_to: Replying to Adversarial Attack across Datasets
display_title: Official Review of Paper2341 by Reviewer G5E5

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an algorithm, Image Classiﬁcation Eraser (ICE), to perform transfer-based adversarial attack across different datasets. ICE involves a meta learning to learn to model on which performing adversarial attack leads to a generlized adversarial example for different datasets. The algorithm is mainly based on MTA, while additional techniques are also proposed to solve the problem of inconstitent labels and input sizes.
content.main_review:
Pros
1. Performing adversarial attack across datasets is a practical problem. For practical models used for the real application, the training set is actually not available to the attacker. And the attacker needs to attack the models trained with domain shifts.

2. Using the meta learning to perform the attack across datasets is natural and reasonable. After seeing different datasets, the trained model may be able to learn the invariant features across the datasets so that it can transfer to the unseen datasets.

3. The experiments do show that ICE leads a large improvement compared with the baselines.

Cons.
1. The authors miss some important baselines that also focus on the attack across datasets [1, 2]. [1] studies the targeted attack with non-overlapping labels. It uses FDA and the pesudo labels to transfer the adversarial examples to different dataset. [2] shows the self-supervised training can be used to train a model to perform transfer-based attack. In this setting, one only needs to collect a few images of the target domain to train a self-supervised model. The model can be used as a surrogate model as trained with the classification loss on the target domain. These two methods should be compared with ICE.

2. The paper only evaluate the effectiveness of ICE on un-targeted attack. It seems that the entropy the ICE uses is not able to perform targeted attack. Targeted attack has lower transferablity and it is more important than the un-targeted attack.

3. ICE should be evaluted on the larger dataset like ImageNet.

4. In section 4.1, the assumption that the catagory of $x$ is unavailble is unreasonable. For the given image, we can classify the image with human eyes. Therefore, the strongest baselines should use this information to peform attack with real label. For the models that do not have the grouthtruth label of $x$, entropy loss may be a substitute loss.

5. The technical contribution of the paper is limited. ICE is technically similar to MTA. They both use meta learning and customized PGD. The difference is choice of tasks. MTA chooses different networks as different tasks for meta learning while ICE chooses different datasets as as different tasks for meta learning.

Minors
1. In section 4.4, sbusection should be subsection.
2. As the paper is discussing an adversarial attack, which may bring safety issues to the current machine learning systems, it has some potential negative impacts.  The authors should discuss more about the ethics issues in the statement.

[1] Nathan Inkawhich et.al. Can Targeted Adversarial Examples Transfer When the Source and Target Models Have No Label Space Overlap?, ICCV 2021
[2] Qizhang Li et.al. Practical No-box Adversarial Attacks against DNNs, NeurIPS 2020
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper works on a interesting problem with a reasonable algorithm. The experiments show that ICE has large improvement compared with some baselines. However, the technical novelty of ICE is limited and the empirical evaluation is incomplete. Therefore, I recommend for rejection at the current phase.

ICE contributes to the adversarial attack and robustness community from a different angle compared with MTA.
As Figure 5 shows, the perturbation noise maps generated by ICE differ greatly from those generated by baselines, and the noise maps generated by ICE share a similar pattern for different images.
This indicates that ICE tries to learn generalizable perturbation pattern that can be applied to images sampled from different categories.
This possibly inspires the community to improve the neural network robustness by simply adding the generalizable noise map to the training set.
Therefore, the contribution of ICE is enough to be accepted by ICLR in our viewpoint.

content.title: Response to question: The assumption that the catagory of x is unavailble is unreasonable. For the given image, we can classify the image with human eyes.
content.comment:
Thanks for your question.
Truly humans can classify the given image and can tell the attacker the image category.
But **it is impractical to classify all captured images by human eye.**
Furthermore, **the generalized transferable attack problem requires the attackers to automatically disturb any captured images that will be fed into unknown image classifiers, without human assistance and the image information.**
Therefore the proposed ICE and all baselines cannot access the real label in generalized transferable attack.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2341 by Reviewer G5E5
display_title: Response to question: The paper only evaluate the effectiveness of ICE on un-targeted attack. It seems that the entropy the ICE uses is not able to perform targeted attack.

content.title: Response to question: The paper only evaluate the effectiveness of ICE on un-targeted attack. It seems that the entropy the ICE uses is not able to perform targeted attack.
content.comment:
Targeted attack conflicts with the proposed generalized transfer attack (GTA) problem.
**In generalized transfer attack, the label set of the unknown target model is inaccessible to the attacker, which means the attacker does not know whether the target label is included in the target model's label set.**
GTA requires the attacker to disturb all possibly encountered images so that any unknown target models predicting these images will make wrong predictions. The goal of GTA is to attack all possibly encountered images and to destroy the classification information of these images. **GTA does not care about which model will be the target model. It only needs to disturb the encountered images**. In other words, **the attack objective in GTA is images rather than unknown target models**, and the target models used in our work is only used to evaluate the GTA performance. 
We cannot know randomly encountered images in advance and will not know the information of the target models predicting the encountered images. 
Therefore, the attacker cannot know the label set of the target model and targeted attack is not well-defined in GTA. 
However, we also agree that there could be some applications when the attacker can guess the label set of the target model, and this will be an interesting direction in our future work.

display_title: Response to question: Some other baselines that also focus on the attack across datasets

content.title: Response to question: Some other baselines that also focus on the attack across datasets
content.comment:
Thanks for your remind and question.
UAP[1] is a newer method that focuses on the attack across datasets.
Therefore we implemented UAP during the rebuttal window. 
In this experiment, we use Cifar-10 and ResNet-18 as the source dataset and the source model, and train the universal adversarial perturbation by minimizing the cosine similarity between 
$f(x)$ and $f(x+\delta)$, where $f$ is the ResNet-18 model.
$x$ and $\delta$ are the clean image and the perturbation.
Then we use the trained $\delta$ to disturb the images from Cifar-100 and attack Cifar-100 models. 
$L_\infty$ perturbation scale of $\delta$ is set to 15/255, which is consistent with the default setting in our work.
The attack success rates on the target models MobileNet-V3, VGG-16, ResNet-18, ResNet-34, SeResNet-26, and DenseNet-26 are:  
UAP: 53.6%, 66.8%, 68.2%, **66.5%**, 59.3%, and 77.0%, respectively.  
ICE: **54.9%**, **67.3%**, **71.5%**, 64.0%, **61.2%**, and **83.5%**, respectively.  
It is obvious that ICE outperforms UAP in most testing scene.
This experiment will be included in the revision (Section A.5.7).

We conducted another experiment to further compare ICE with UAP.
In this experiment, we use Cifar-10, Tiered$\_{T84}$, and Tiered$\_{V56}$ as the source datasets and use three ResNet-18 models respectively trained on the source datasets as the source models.
Then we disturb the images from Cifar-100.
The attack success rates on the target models MobileNet-V3, VGG-16, ResNet-18, ResNet-34, SeResNet-26, and DenseNet-26 are:  
UAP: 46.5%, 65.6%, 66.3%, 61.6%, 56.8%, and 77.7%, respectively.  
ICE: **56.3%, 83.2%,  90.1%, 87.3%,  80.1%**, and **92.4%**, respectively.  
It is clear that compared with the former experiment, UAP cannot leverage the additional resources to improve its performance. 
As a comparison, the proposed ICE is much more efficient than UAP to leverage the additional resources to improve the performance.
We will conduct more experiments to compare ICE and UAP and will include more comparisons between ICE and UAP in our final version.

[1] Data-Free Universal Adversarial Perturbation and Black-Box Attack (ICCV 2021)

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies a new setting for adversarial attacks: Generalized Transferable Attack, in which the adversary has no source models trained on the same dataset as the victim model. The new setting is more realistic compared with existing transfer-based attacks. The Image  Classification Eraser (ICE) method is then proposed to generate adversarial examples under this setting. A universal model is trained as the surrogate model, and meta-learning algorithm is developed to train the model. Experiments on several datasets show the effectiveness.
content.main_review:
Strength:

- A new adversarial attack setting is proposed to reduce the knowledge of the victim classifier. The adversary needs to generate adversarial examples without access to the training datasets. This setting could be more realistic in practical application.
- To handle this problem, a new attack method is proposed, which is designed to address two problems: 1) the label of testing images cannot be predicted; 2) the shape of testing images is different. A meta-learning algorithm is develop to train the universal surrogate model.
- Initial experiments on several datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

Weaknesses:

- The main weakness lies in the experiments. Three datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, TIered) are used, but these datasets would be quite similar in terms of visual contents, i.e., they contain images of general objects. However, a more realistic setting would be using the datasets with different/diverse visual contents, including digital image classification (MNIST),  face recognition models, etc. Using the diverse datasets can show whether the adversary can succeed under the proposed setting.
- As the paper proposes a meta-learning algorithm, it is better to formulate the bi-level optimization problem to make it clearer.
- It is not clear why the authors use MTA (Eq. (2)) to craft adversarial examples during inner optimization. Can other attacks (e.g., FGSM/PGD) be similarly used?
- Why do you adopt a universal surrogate model? Can you use some kinds of generative models (which input original image and output adversarial one) to generate adversarial examples? 

A related work is missing: "Enhancing Cross-Task Black-Box Transferability of Adversarial Examples with Dispersion Reduction", CVPR 2020.

replying_to: Replying to Thanks for the response
display_title: Response: Explanation of the bi-level optimization framework

content.title: Response: Explanation of the bi-level optimization framework
content.comment:
Thanks for your remind.
The proposed ICE leverages a bi-level optimization framework to train a universal surrogate model to solve the generalized transfer attack problem.
ICE trains a universal surrogate model to achieve the following goal: obtaining particular adversarial perturbations that can effectively erase the classification information of the encountered images by confusing the universal surrogate model.
The proposed bi-level training framework is an effective framework for ICE to achieve the above goal.
**Each bi-level training iteration contains an inner-loop and an outer-loop, and either the inner-loop or the outer-loop contains a gradient-based optimizing process.**
In the inner-loop, we feed the encountered images to the universal surrogate model and disturb these images by confusing the universal surrogate model. 
The encountered images which are simulated by the source images are disturbed by gradient ascent in the inner-loop (Eq.2).
In the outer-loop, we first feed the disturbed images obtained in the inner-loop to the source models and evaluate how these disturbed images are confusing to be classified by feeding them into the source models (Eq.3).
It is known that the larger the prediction losses of the source models, the larger the possibility that the disturbed images are confusing to be classified.
Therefore, in the outer-loop, to ensure that the disturbed images obtained in the inner-loop be confusing, we optimize the universal surrogate model by maximizing the prediction losses of the source models (Eq.4).

The inner-loop can also be understood as the process that generates adversarial examples for the generalized transfer attack problem.
The outer-loop evaluates the generalized transfer attack performances of the generated adversarial examples and improves the performances by optimizing the universal surrogate model.
**Therefore, the inner-loop together with the outer-loop can be understood as a closed loop of adversarial example generation (Eq.2), generalized transfer attack evaluation (Eq.3), generalized transfer attack performance optimization (Eq.4).**

content.title: Response to Reviewer 822A: The experiment that uses CUB resources to attack face recognition models.
content.comment:
Following your valuable suggestion " A more realistic setting would be using the datasets with different/diverse visual contents, including digital image classification (MNIST), face recognition models", we performed another experiment on CUB and CASIA-Webface.
CUB is a fine-grained bird classification dataset and CASIA-Webface is a face recognition dataset containing 10575 identities.
In this experiment, we use CUB as the source dataset, and use the models trained on CUB as source models.
Then we implement baselines and the proposed ICE with the resources and disturb the images from CASIA-Webface.
We split CASIA-Webface into a training and a testing set.
Either the training set or the testing set contains 10575 identities.
The testing set contains the first two facial images or each identity and the training set contains all the other facial images.
The two models DenseNet-26 and SeResNet-26 trained on CASIA-Webface are used as the unknown target models to evaluate the generalized transferable attack performances.
The performances are:   
FGSM:  99.6% and 93.0%;  
PGD:  98.1% and 80.7%;  
MI:  99.6% and 91.1%;  
TI-DIM:  94.0% and 96.3%;  
ICE:  **99.9%** and **96.9%**.  
It is clear that ICE outperforms the baselines to utilize the CUB resources to disturb CASIA-Webface faces.
We will include this experiment in our next version.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers untargeted blackbox transfer attacks, in particular in the relatively underexplored scenario where the target model’s dataset, classes, input resolution are unknown. This paper introduces ICE, whose universal surrogate model is trained to successfully disrupt an ensemble of whitebox models, which may have various architectures, input resolution, or data distribution. By doing so, the hope is that the universal surrogate model can produce adversarial attacks that generalize well, despite not knowing the aforementioned target model characteristics. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated by considering various combinations of datasets (CIFAR-10/100, TieredImageNet) and CNN architectures, outperforming a number of baselines adapted to the setting.
content.main_review:
Pros:
-	Considers an underexplored, challenging, and realistic setting in adversarial attacks
-	Flexible to input/output dimension, labels
-	Formulation/training of universal surrogate model is reasonable and fairly clever; I don’t think it’s something I’ve seen before in the attack literature
-	Proposed method can take advantage of multiple models/datasets to get better performance while the baselines cannot.
-	Relatively thorough experiments comparing against several baselines across multiple model architectures and datasets
-	Clearly written and presented

Cons:
-	Overstated claims of novelty of the problem setting
-	An ensemble of source models during training increases computation cost
-	Universal surrogate model must be trained, which adds extra prep and complexity versus just using an off-the-shelf pre-trained whitebox model.
-	Untargeted attack, which is easier and provides less control to an attacker than targeted attacks.
-	Ethics statement is overly simplistic

Detailed Comments

Novelty of the setting:
While it is true that the prevailing assumption in previous blackbox transfer attacks, the claim that *all* methods assume that the white-box model is trained on the same dataset as the blackbox model is not true. For example, [1] considers the setting where the blackbox and whitebox models share none of the training samples, and [2] explores settings where there are no overlap in labels. This setting has also been referred to as “no-box” or “data-free” as well [3,4]. While I’m not saying the existence of prior work necessarily render this work completely moot, the claims being made nonetheless need to be adjusted: in particular, the authors should be careful with the use of the words “all” and “none”, and discussions/empirical comparisons (“no existing methods can be directly used as baselines”) of these previous works should be added.


Experiments:
1.	Overall, the experiments are fairly well-designed, demonstrating that the proposed method can effectively take advantage of both additional datasets and architectures, which the compared baselines cannot. The proposed method outperforms the baselines at untargeted attacks. Ideally, there would also be comparison with other similar methods: e.g. see comments above on novelty of the setting, or knowledge distillation below.
2.	While they’re not identical, there’s a decent amount of overlap between the labels of CIFAR10 + CIFAR100 and TieredImageNet. I wish the authors had better teased out the relationship between label overlap and overall attack performance, or considered datasets with less overlap (e.g. CUB birds -> cat and dogs, or animals -> cars or planes).
3.	How does the universal surrogate model compare with a model that learns to combine sources through knowledge distillation? 
4.	I’m not sure if the proposed method of adapting GTA to the baselines necessarily shows them in the best light. In particular, resizing and averaging the adversarial samples may suppress their individual perturbations and mess up their effectiveness. Why not optimize for a single adversarial example that maximizes the entropy for all the networks?

Ethics Statement:
There’s an extensive literature when it comes to adversarial attacks, and the potential negative societal impacts of adversarial attacks have been discussed quite a bit. This work is not unique in exposing such concerns, but I do think the authors should spend a little more time discussing the potential impact of their work, especially since the proposed attack setting is (relatively) new. Claiming “no potential negative societal impacts” doesn’t demonstrate very much thought.

Miscellaneous:
1.	Citing just MAML (Finn 2017) for the introduction of the proposed “bi-level training framework” is an odd choice. I think the authors are trying to draw similarities between the proposed method’s inner and outer loop with meta-learning, but there are other meta-learning methods that are perhaps a closer analogy than MAML, which optimizes model weights in the inner loop (ICE does not).
2.	The numbered step-by-step description in the latter half of Section 4.1 is a little sloppy, with a mix of complete sentences describing what the authors did and imperative sentences. I’d recommend reformatting all to the former. 
3.	Section 4.4: “sbusection"
4.	Table 4 out of order compared to Section 4.5

Other questions:
1.	Visually (Figure 5), the proposed attack appears to generate different looking noise when compared to the other methods. Any thoughts why this might be the case?
2.	What is ICE’s advantage over the baseline methods when using a single model and dataset (i.e. the first set of rows in Table 2)? The performance seems significantly better, even without taking advantage of multiple models and datasets. How does ICE compare to state-of-the-art in the more standard query-free blackbox setting?



[1] “Perturbing Across the Feature Hierarchy to Improve Standard and Strict Blackbox Attack Transferability”, NeurIPS 2020

[2] “Can Targeted Adversarial Examples Transfer When the Source and Target Models Have No Label Space Overlap?” ICCVw 2021

[3] “Practical No-box Adversarial Attacks against DNNs”, NeurIPS 2020

[4] “Data-Free Universal Adversarial Perturbation and Black-Box Attack”, ICCV 2021


=====Discussion Phase Update=====

I thank the authors for all the effort they put in during the rebuttal phase, especially for all the new experiments that were done. I bump my score up slightly to marginally above the acceptance threshold, though I do think this paper could also still benefit from another round of review. A good deal of my concerns have been addressed, but a lot of work still needs to be done on the paper. Regardless of what the final decision is, please do try to work in the suggestions made here by the various reviewers for the next version.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this paper explores a challenging and practical attack setting, proposing an interesting and reasonable method to achieve good untargeted attack rates. While it is indeed underexplored, there are repeated overclaims on the novelty of the proposed setting. Regardless, even though the problem setting isn’t novel, the proposed method suffices as a good contribution. I question how fairly the baselines are portrayed, and some other important baselines are missing, but overall the experiments are well-designed and get good results. I rate this paper just under the threshold, but I’m willing to raise my score if my concerns are addressed.

content.title: Response to question: Visually (Figure 5), the proposed attack appears to generate different looking noise when compared to the other methods. Any thoughts why this might be the case?
content.comment:
It is very interesting to see that the perturbation noise generated by ICE differs greatly from those generated by the other methods.
The possible reason for this phenomenon is that ICE is trained to maximize the prediction entropy without using labels.
In other words, **ICE needs to disturb the input image without knowing the groundtruth classification information, which forces ICE to learn some perturbation pattern that correlates little with groundtruth information.**

In Figure 5, we can see that **ICE generates similar perturbation noises for different input images, which means ICE may learn a particular perturbation pattern that is generalizable across different image categories.**
In our opinion, learning a generalizable perturbation pattern may be a straightforward way for ICE to solve generalized transfer attack.
The visualization may remind us that **it is possible to find a universal perturbation pattern that can solve generalized transfer attack, which can be regarded as another contribution of ICE.**
The visualization may also help us to understand and improve the robustness of DNNs.

content.title: Response to question: Untargeted attack, which is easier and provides less control to an attacker than targeted attacks.
content.comment:
Targeted attack conflicts with the proposed generalized transfer attack problem.
**In generalized transfer attack, the label set of the unknown target model is inaccessible to the attacker, which means the attacker does not know whether the target label is included in the target model's label set.**
Generalized transfer attack is the problem that the attacker needs to disturb all encountered images and wishes the adversarial images will fool the unknown target models predicting these images.
The setting assumes zero information of the target model and target label set, 
**thus targeted attack is unavailable in generalized transfer attack.**
However, we agree with the reviewer that there could be some applications when the attacker can guess the label set of the target model, and this will be an interesting future direction.

content.title: Response to question: Why not optimize for a single adversarial example that maximizes the entropy for all the networks?
content.comment:
Thanks for your advice.
To try your advice, we re-implement PGD-based baselines, and these baselines perturb the input image $x$ by performing the following pipeline for $T$ iterations.
The $i$-th iteration contains the following three steps.
	
1. We resize the image $x^{(i-1)}$ to the input shapes of all source models and then feed the resized images to the source models, respectively. 
$x^{(i-1)}$ is the perturbed image generated in the $i-1$ iteration and $x^{(0)}=x$.
Then the inference of $x^{(i-1)}$ on one source model $M_{D_k}^j$ can be formulated as $y_{D_k}^j$ = $M_{D_k}^j(x_{D_k}^j)$, where $x_{D_k}^j$ = $resize(x^{(i-1)}, resolution(M_{D_k}^j))$ is the resized image for the source model $M_{D_k}^j$. 
2. We calculate the prediction losses of all the source models with the formulation $L = \frac{1}{m} \cdot \sum_{k=1}^{m} \cdot \big ( \frac{1}{N_k} \cdot  \sum_{j=1}^{N_k}\mathcal{L}(y_{D_k}^{j}) \big)$, where $\mathcal{L}$ is entropy.  
3. We disturb the input image $x^{(i-1)}$ with the formulation $x^{(i)} =  \text{clip}(x^{(i-1)} + \frac{\epsilon}{T} \cdot \delta )$, where $\delta = \text{sign}\big (\nabla_{x^{(i-1)}}{L} \big )$.
	
After $T$ iterations, we obtain the disturbed image $x^{(T)}$, and feed it and the clean image $x$ into the unknown target model $\mathbb{M}$ and get its predictions. The GTA process is successful if $\mathbb{M}(x^{(T)}) \neq \mathbb{M}(x)$.

We perform an experiment to evaluate how the re-implemented PGD-based baselines perform on GTA. In this experiment, Cifar-10, Tiered$\_{T84}$, and Tiered$\_{V56}$ are used as source datasets, and three ResNet-18 respectively trained on the three datasets are used as the source models.
The experimental results on the target models MobileNet-V3, VGG-16, ResNet-18, ResNet-34, SeResNet-26,and DenseNet-26 are:   
FGSM: 47.5%, 63.2%, 56.3%, 55.5%, 58.2%, 72.6%;   
PGD:  38.8%, 53.6%, 43.1%, 43.1%, 47.5%, 64.6%;   
DI:   38.6%, 53.9%, 43.3%, 42.8%, 47.7%, 64.7%;  
MI:   46.2%, 62.8%, 53.8%, 52.7%, 56.6%, 71.9%;   
TI-DIM: 47.9%, 43.8%, 44.9%, 45.1%, 44.2%, 54.0%;  
**Compared with the results in the last row of Table 2, optimizing a single image improves FGSM and MI, but damages DI and TI-DIM.**
Optimizing a single adversarial image to address the generalized transfer attack problem cannot stably improve the baselines.
This experiment will be included in our revision (Section A.5.4).

Furthermore, as the experiment in the first row of Table 2 shows, the proposed ICE outperforms the baselines when only a single source model and a single source dataset can be used.
In this case, no average operation is needed to get the adversarial image, and the performances of baselines will not be influenced by the average operations.
**In conclusion, the proposed ICE outperforms the baselines no matter the existence of average operation in baselines.**

content.title: Response to question: Training the universal surrogate model needs more computation cost.
content.comment:
It is true that training the universal surrogate model increases the computation cost in the training stage.
**But to disturb input image in inference, ICE costs fewer computation resources than baselines, which is another advantage of ICE.**
This is because the proposed ICE needs to confuse only the universal surrogate model in inference, while the baselines need to simultaneously confuse all the source models.
Confusing multiple models needs to calculate the gradient in all the source models while confusing a single model needs to calculate the gradient only in one model.
**As Section A.6 shows, ICE greatly saves the inference cost, compared with PGD-based baselines.**

content.title: Reply to Author Comments
content.comment:
Thank you for the responses.

I appreciate the experiments optimizing the loss across the ensemble as opposed to individually and summing the perturbations. I’m a little surprised the results aren’t better, but it is what it is.

I understand the authors’ point that their set up doesn’t assume knowing the target model’s label space. However, this was a choice made for this particular set up, and not one that I find completely reasonable. If one wants to attack a model, the attacker should probably at least have an idea of what the model is for and thus should be able to guess at least some of target labels, which implies a targeted attack should be possible.. Regardless of whether the labels are known though, it is still generally true that an untargeted attack is less useful than a targeted one.

The comment on universal perturbations is a potentially interesting one. What happens when changing the objective from maximizing entropy on one particular image to trying to produce a universal perturbation? There probably isn't enough time before the end of the discussion period to try it (so please don't take this as an expectation), but I encourage the authors to explore this idea further.

Reviewer G5E5 shared my concerns on similarity of the proposed GTA setting with other papers, but I haven’t seen any acknowledgement from the authors or changes to the submission. The claims in the paper of novelty and of the lack of baselines are not true, and without changes to the way it’s presented, certain parts of this paper are incorrect and misleading. 

“ICE is trained to disturb source images without knowing label” => This is also true of the baseline methods’ generation process of the adversarial perturbations as described in 4.1 (“we generate adversarial perturbation by maximizing the entropy”). Thus, it doesn’t seem like not knowing the label explains the better performance of ICE.

Finally, in the future, please try to consolidate your responses into fewer posts to cut down on notification spam.

content.title: Response to Reviewer o3fm
content.comment:
Thanks very much for your reply. 
I have revised our manuscript and have updated the revised version. Thanks for your checking.

### 1. More explanation about the experiment that optimizes a single adversarial example for GTA.
Here we try to explain why optimizing a single adversarial example cannot improve baselines.
Suppose there are three source models respectively trained on Cifar-10, Tiered$\_{T84}$, and Tiered$\_{V56}$, maybe the following reasons can explain the experimental results.   
1). **There still exist implicit resizing operations when we optimize a single adversarial image (the gradient propagates through resizing layers) at each gradient ascent step**. With the three source datasets, each gradient ascent step needs 3 explicit and 3 implicit resizing operations in the forward and backward paths, respectively.   
2). Optimizing a single adversarial image needs to fuse the gradients from all the three source models at each gradient ascent step. This may result in that the single adversarial example $x^{(i-1)}$ obtained in the $i-1$ step being not optima and accurate to attack each source model due to the implicit resizing operations, and further influences the following gradient ascent steps.   
3). As introduced in Section 4.1, **the default implementation of baselines explicitly resizes the adversarial images only before the first and only after the last gradient ascent steps**. For example, when using the Cifar-10 model to generate the perturbation, we explicitly resize the image $x$ to the resolution of Cifar-10 model only before the first gradient ascent step, and explicitly resize the adversarial example on the Cifar-10 model back into the original resolution of $x$ only after the last gradient ascent step. Therefore, between the first and the last step, there are no resizing operations to influence the adversarial effectiveness of the adversarial examples generated on the Cifar-10,  Tiered$\_{T84}$, and Tiered$\_{V56}$ models, respectively. 

The experiment shows that FGSM can be improved by optimizing a single adversarial image.
FGSM contains a single gradient ascent step, which means the first and the last gradient ascent steps is the same step.
When optimizing a single adversarial image, FGSM has 3 implicit and 3 explicit resizing operations, while when using the default implementation introduced in Section 4.1, FGSM contains 3x2=6 explicit resizing operations. In our opinion, gradient fusing through implicit resizing operations is more accurate than through explicit resizing operations.

PGD contains 10 gradient ascent steps in our work.
When optimizing a single adversarial image, PGD has 3x10=30 implicit and 3x10=30 explicit resizing operations, while when using the default implementation introduced in Section 4.1, PGD contains 3x2=6 explicit resizing operations, which needs less resizing. In our opinion, the more the number of explicit resizing operations, the worse the GTA performance, and this is the reason why optimizing a single adversarial image at each gradient ascent step damages PGD.

### 2. More explanation about the GTA setting
GTA is the setting where the attacker needs to disturb all possibly encountered images so that any unknown target models predicting these images will make wrong predictions. The goal of GTA is to attack all possibly encountered images and to destroy the classification information of these images. **GTA does not care about which model will be the target model. It only needs to disturb the encountered images**. In other words, **the attack objective in GTA is images rather than unknown target models**, and the target models used in our work is only used to evaluate the GTA performance. Therefore, we currently assume the setting that the attacker has zero information about the label set of target model, so it's hard to define targeted attack in this case. However, we agree with the reviewer that there could be some applications when the attacker can guess the label set of the target model, and this will be an interesting future direction.

### 3. Novelty and the lack of baselines.
We have implemented UAP[1] in the rebuttal and have included the results in Section A.5.7. Due to the time limitation of the rebuttal, we only tested it on one GTA scene. We will test UAP on all the other scenes after rebuttal and will include all the results of UAP in Tables 1 and 2.

### 4. Explanation of the better performance of ICE
Sorry for the confusion. The ICE model is trained to maximize the performance of GTA attack (the inner maximization is mimicking GTA attack). However, other methods use normally trained surrogate model and standard attack objective (when assuming label sets are available) and transfer the obtained adversarial examples to the GTA attack setting. Therefore, it's natural that ICE outperforms baselines as it considered GTA attack when training the universal surrogate model.

content.comment:
## Question: 
How does the universal surrogate model compare with a model that learns to combine sources through knowledge distillation?
### Response:
We performed another experiment in rebuttal to answer your question.
In this experiment, we use Cifar-10, Tiered$\_{T84}$, and Tiered$\_{V56}$ as source datasets, and use three ResNet-18 respectively trained on the source datasets as source models.
First, we build another model $G$ that has three heads corresponding to the three source datasets.
The backbone of $G$ is the same as that of the proposed ICE (Shown in Figure 4).
The first head that has 10 output nodes is used to classify Cifar-10 images.
The second head which has 351 output nodes is used to classify Tiered$\_{T84}$ images.
The third head which has 257 output nodes is used to classify Tiered$\_{V56}$ images.
Second, we use the three source models and three datasets to train $G$ with offline knowledge distillation.
The model $G$ obtains test accuracies of 97.5%, 61.7%, and 70.3% on Cifar-10, Tiered$\_{T84}$, and Tiered$\_{V56}$, respectively.
Finally, we use the baseline methods and model $G$ to disturb the images from Cifar-100.
The GTA success rates on the target models MobileNet-V3, VGG-16, ResNet-18, ResNet-34, SeResNet-26, and DenseNet-26 are:  
FGSM:  46.4%, 59.6%, 51.0%, 51.4%, 55.1%, and 70.6%.  
PGD: 36.9%, 49.6%, 40.3%, 40.1%, 43.4%, and 61.3%.  
MI: 43.9%, 56.6%, 47.6%, 47.3%, 52.4%, and 68.4%.  
TI: 49.2%, 43.7%, 45.9%, 46.5%, 44.6%, and 54.4%.  
Compared with the results in the first row of Table 2, we can conclude that using knowledge-distillation to obtain a single model $G$ cannot improve the GTA performances of baselines.
This experiment will be included in the revision (Section A.5.6).

## Question:
I wish the authors had better teased out the relationship between label overlap and overall attack performance, or considered datasets with less overlap (e.g. CUB birds -> cat and dogs, or animals -> cars or planes).
### Response:
Thanks for your question.
We performed a novel experiment to address your concern.
In this experiment, the source dataset and source model are Cifar-10 and ResNet-18 respectively, and the target dataset is CUB, which is a fine-grained image classification dataset and differs greatly from Cifar-10.
The target models are ResNet-18 and DenseNet-26 trained on CUB.
The two target models use a consistent input resolution of 112x112 and achieve approximately 54.9% and 48.3% accuracies.
The attack success rate on the two target models are:  
FGSM: 22.7%, 32.6%;  
PGD: 17.2%  24.3%;  
MI: 21.9%, 30.8%;  
DI: 49.1%, 72.5%;  
TI-DIM: 62.8%, 73.4%;  
**ICE: 65.1%, 87.0%**  
Clearly, ICE performs the best to disturb the images from CUB by using Cifar-10.
We will include this experiment in our revision (Section A.5.5).

## Quesion: 
Overstated claims of novelty of the problem setting.
### Response:  
Thanks for your remind and question.
We have revised our writing to avoid overclaiming of our novelty.
UAP[1] is the newest method in all your mentioned papers.
Therefore, due to the time limitation, we only implemented UAP during the rebuttal window. 
In this experiment, we use Cifar-10 and ResNet-18 as the source dataset and the source model, and train the universal adversarial perturbation by minimizing the cosine similarity between $f(x)$ and $f(x+\delta)$, where $f$ is the ResNet-18 model.
$x$ and $\delta$ are the clean image and the perturbation, respectively.
Then we use the trained $\delta$ to disturb the images from Cifar-100 and attack Cifar-100 models. 
$L_\infty$ perturbation scale of $\delta$ is set to 15/255, which is consistent with the default setting in our work.
The attack success rates on the target models MobileNet-V3, VGG-16, ResNet-18, ResNet-34, SeResNet-26, and DenseNet-26 are:  
UAP: 53.6%, 66.8%, 68.2%, **66.5%**, 59.3%, and 77.0%, respectively.  
ICE: **54.9%**, **67.3%**, **71.5%**, 64.0%, **61.2%**, and **83.5%**, respectively.  
It is obvious that ICE outperforms UAP in most testing scene.
This experiment will be included in the revision (Section A.5.7).
After the rebuttal, we will conduct more experiments to compare ICE and UAP, and these comparisons will be shown in the final version.

> [1] Data-Free Universal Adversarial Perturbation and Black-Box Attack (ICCV 2021)

display_title: Official Review of Paper2341 by Reviewer ggdd

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper describes a new adversarial attack setting called “Generalized Transferrable Attacks” (GTA). The goal of GTA is to create transferrable adversarial examples in the black-box setting without query access and without access to surrogate models trained on the target data distribution. The paper proposes a novel attack called “Image Classification Eraser” (ICE), which allows the creation of transferable examples for any arbitrary dataset. ICE trains a “universal model” that has good adversarial transferability for surrogate datasets using a meta-learning objective and uses this model to create transferable adversarial examples.
content.main_review:
**Strengths**
1. The problem setting of Generalized Transferrable Attacks is well motivated and novel.
2. I found the solution of creating a universal surrogate model using a meta-learning objective to be interesting.
3. The paper is well-written and the figures make it easy to follow.

**Concerns**

1. Evaluation against Defenses

The proposed attack has not been evaluated against any defenses. Given the novelty of the threat model, I don’t think this is sufficient to disqualify the paper. However, I would have liked to see the proposed attack evaluated against simple defenses such as adversarial training.

2. Choice of loss function for baseline evaluations

The adv. example for the baseline evaluations is created by maximizing the entropy of f(\hat{x}). While this does maximize the uncertainty in the model’s predictions, it does not maximally change the model’s prediction (which is the goal of creating adv. examples). Section 4.5.2 tries to address this concern by treating the model’s original argmax prediction: argmax(y) as the pseudo label. However, the authors could have taken this idea a step further by considering the model’s original softmax prediction (y) as the soft pseudo label and maximizing the KL divergence between y (the model’s original softmax predictions) and f(\hat{x}). Did you consider using this alternative loss function for creating adv examples? I think the effectiveness of the baseline attacks would improve with this alternative loss function. Can you justify this choice of loss function for the baseline evaluations?



3. Baseline evaluation with multiple source models: 

The authors suggest using the following method for creating adv examples for the baseline case with multiple source models:
Create adv examples individually for each of the source models
Average the adv examples from step 1 to create a single adv example.
I’m not convinced that the averaged example (from step 2) remains adversarial for all the source models. This also possibly explains why the results for baseline do not improve with additional source models. A better way to create adv examples for multiple models would be to optimize a single image and make it adversarial across the ensemble of source models. 

**Nit**

Abstract: “differente datasets” -> “different datasets”
content.summary_of_the_review: I have some concerns about the evaluations in this paper. However, I recommend that the paper be accepted mainly because of the novelty of the threat model.

2. We calculate the prediction losses of all the source models with the formulation $L = \frac{1}{m} \cdot \sum_{k=1}^{m} \cdot \big ( \frac{1}{N_k} \cdot  \sum_{j=1}^{N_k}\mathcal{L}(y_{D_k}^{j}) \big)$, where $\mathcal{L}$ is entropy.  
3. We disturb the input image $x^{(i-1)}$ with the formulation $x^{(i)} =  \text{clip}(x^{(i-1)} + \frac{\epsilon}{T} \cdot \delta )$, where $\delta = \text{sign}\big (\nabla_{x^{(i-1)}}{L} \big )$.
	
After $T$ iterations, we obtain the disturbed image $x^{(T)}$, and feed it and the clean image $x$ into the unknown target model $\mathbb{M}$ and get its predictions. The GTA process is successful if $\mathbb{M}(x^{(T)}) \neq \mathbb{M}(x)$.

We perform an experiment to evaluate how the re-implemented PGD-based baselines perform on GTA. In this experiment, Cifar-10, Tiered$\_{T84}$, and Tiered$\_{V56}$ are used as source datasets, and three ResNet-18 respectively trained on the three datasets are used as the source models.
The experimental results on the target models MobileNet-V3, VGG-16, ResNet-18, ResNet-34, SeResNet-26,and DenseNet-26 are:   
FGSM: 47.5%, 63.2%, 56.3%, 55.5%, 58.2%, 72.6%;   
PGD:  38.8%, 53.6%, 43.1%, 43.1%, 47.5%, 64.6%;   
DI:   38.6%, 53.9%, 43.3%, 42.8%, 47.7%, 64.7%;  
MI:   46.2%, 62.8%, 53.8%, 52.7%, 56.6%, 71.9%;   
TI-DIM: 47.9%, 43.8%, 44.9%, 45.1%, 44.2%, 54.0%;  
**Compared with the results in the last row of Table 2, optimizing a single image improves FGSM and MI, but damages DI and TI-DIM.**
Optimizing a single adversarial image to address the generalized transfer attack problem cannot stably improve the baselines.
This experiment will be included in our revision (Section A.5.4).

Furthermore, as the experiment in the first row of Table 2 shows, the proposed ICE outperforms the baselines when only a single source model and a single source dataset can be used.
In this case, no average operation is needed to get the adversarial image, and the performances of baselines will not be influenced by the average operations.
**In conclusion, the proposed ICE outperforms the baselines no matter the existence of average operation in baselines.**

display_title: Response to authors

content.title: Response to authors
content.comment: Thanks for carrying out additional experiments. The results do seem to address my concerns. I am, however, a little surprised that, for some of the attacks, the method of averaging adversarial examples from individual models performs better than jointly optimizing a single image across all models. Any thoughts on why this is the case?

replying_to: Replying to Response to authors
display_title: Response to Reviewer ggdd

content.title: Response to Reviewer ggdd
content.comment:
Thanks for your timely reply.

Suppose there are three source models respectively trained on Cifar-10, Tiered$\_{T84}$, and Tiered$\_{V56}$, maybe the following reasons can explain why optimizing a single adversarial example cannot improve baselines.   
1. **There still exist implicit resizing operations when we optimize a single adversarial image (the gradient propagates through resizing layers) at each gradient ascent step**. With the three source datasets, each gradient ascent step needs 3 explicit and 3 implicit resizing operations in the forward and backward paths, respectively.   
2. Optimizing a single adversarial image needs to fuse the gradients from all the three source models at each gradient ascent step. This may result in that the single adversarial example $x^{(i-1)}$ obtained in the $i-1$ step being not optima and accurate to attack each source model due to the implicit resizing operations, and further influences the following gradient ascent steps.   
3. As introduced in Section 4.1, **the default implementation of baselines explicitly resizes the adversarial images only before the first and only after the last gradient ascent steps**. For example, when using the Cifar-10 model to generate the perturbation, we explicitly resize the image $x$ to the resolution of Cifar-10 model only before the first gradient ascent step, and explicitly resize the adversarial example on the Cifar-10 model back into the original resolution of $x$ only after the last gradient ascent step. Therefore, between the first and the last step, there are no resizing operations to influence the adversarial effectiveness of the adversarial examples generated on the Cifar-10,  Tiered$\_{T84}$, and Tiered$\_{V56}$ models, respectively. 

The experiment shows that FGSM can be improved by optimizing a single adversarial image, which may prove the three reasons.
FGSM contains a single gradient ascent step, which means the first and the last gradient ascent steps is the same step.
When optimizing a single adversarial image, FGSM has 3 implicit and 3 explicit resizing operations, while when using the default implementation introduced in Section 4.1, FGSM contains 3x2=6 explicit resizing operations. In our opinion, gradient fusing through implicit resizing operations is more accurate than through explicit resizing operations, and this is the reason why FGSM can be improved by optimizing a single adversarial image.

The experiment also shows that PGD can be damaged by optimizing a single adversarial image.
PGD contains 10 gradient ascent steps in our work.
When optimizing a single adversarial image, PGD has 3x10=30 implicit and 3x10=30 explicit resizing operations, while when using the default implementation introduced in Section 4.1, PGD contains 3x2=6 explicit resizing operations, which needs less resizing. In our opinion, the more the number of explicit resizing operations, the worse the GTA performance, and this is the reason why optimizing a single adversarial image at each gradient ascent step damages PGD.

We hope that our response has addressed your concerns, and if you have other comments, we are glad to address them.
